planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring into humus-rich, acidic, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil in a sheltered, dappled-shade woodland site protected from wind and late frost.

directions: Rhododendron thomsonii is grown for its waxy, blood-red, bell-shaped flowers held in loose trusses in mid-spring, set off by smooth, rounded, blue-green leaves that lack the felted indumentum typical of many big-leaf Himalayan species. With age the smooth, plum-to-cinnamon bark flakes away in patches, adding winter interest to what eventually becomes a small gnarled tree. Native to the forests of Sikkim, Bhutan, and the Tibet-Himalaya border around 2700-3400m, it wants a sheltered woodland position with filtered light, since its smooth leaves scorch readily in strong sun or drying wind. Grow in deep, humus-rich, consistently moist acidic soil and avoid open, exposed sites.

common_name: Griffith's Rhododendron (Giant Fragrant White Himalayan Species)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring into fertile, humus-rich, acidic soil in a sheltered woodland site with dappled shade; buds swell early and need protection from late frost.

directions: Rhododendron griffithianum bears some of the largest and most fragrant flowers of any species rhododendron, with loose trusses of broad white blooms that can reach six inches across in spring, set against thin, smooth, somewhat drooping leaves and attractive peeling reddish-brown bark. Native to forest at roughly 2100-3000m in Sikkim, Bhutan, and the Darjeeling hills, it is one of the key parents behind many large-flowered hybrid rhododendrons, including the fragrant Loderi group. It is less cold-hardy than many Himalayan companions and needs a mild, sheltered woodland site out of wind, with deep, moist, humus-rich acidic soil, since both the plant and its early flower buds are vulnerable to hard frost.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring into well-drained, humus-rich acidic soil in part shade; this species tolerates more sun and better drainage than big-leaf Himalayan rhododendrons.

directions: Rhododendron cinnabarinum carries waxy, tubular to bell-shaped flowers that open in loose, nodding clusters in late spring, typically in shades of cinnabar-red, apricot, or plum, though some populations and the well-known Concatenans Group run toward yellow and orange. The rounded, blue-green leaves are aromatic when crushed, a useful identification trait among Himalayan species. Native to forest margins and open slopes from Sikkim and Bhutan into southeastern Tibet at roughly 2700-3700m, it is more tolerant of sun and drier footing than its big-leaf relatives, making it a good upright companion shrub planted among smaller rhododendrons and understory perennials. Give it humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil and shelter from the harshest winter wind.

common_name: Bell Rhododendron (Indumented Lilac Bell-Flowered Himalayan Species)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring into humus-rich, moisture-retentive, acidic soil in dappled woodland shade sheltered from wind.

directions: Rhododendron campanulatum produces rounded trusses of bell-shaped flowers in shades of lilac-purple fading toward white, each marked with a darker purple blotch, opening in mid to late spring. The thick, leathery leaves carry a dense fawn-to-cinnamon felt of indumentum on their undersides, a texture typical of many high-elevation Himalayan species. Found from Kashmir east to Bhutan at roughly 3000-3600m, it often forms dense understory thickets beneath conifers and larger tree rhododendrons in its native forest. It is among the hardier big-leaf Himalayan species and tolerates somewhat heavier soil than most, but still performs best in cool, humid summers with consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil and protection from drying wind.

planting.note: Pot into a very free-draining, bark- or moss-based mix and site in bright, sheltered part shade; in cold-winter climates grow it in a container that can move to a cool, humid greenhouse for winter.

directions: Rhododendron edgeworthii is grown above all for its powerfully fragrant flowers, large and white with a pink flush on the reverse, opening amid deeply veined, bristly dark green leaves backed with a woolly brown indumentum. In its native forests of Sikkim, Bhutan, and Yunnan, at roughly 1800-3000m, it grows naturally as an epiphyte or lithophyte on mossy tree trunks and rock ledges rather than rooted in ordinary soil. This loose, sprawling, somewhat untidy shrub is best grown in a raised bed, large pot, or hanging basket filled with an extremely free-draining, humus-rich mix that mimics its perched habitat, and it needs reliably high humidity. Outside mild, frost-free maritime climates it is usually grown under glass, since it is markedly less cold-hardy than most other Himalayan forest rhododendrons.

planting.note: Start seed indoors on the surface of the mix since it needs light to germinate, then set out transplants into cool, moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; most forms flower once after two or three seasons and then die.

directions: Satin poppy forms a low rosette densely covered in rusty-brown bristly hairs, from which a tall, leafy flowering stem eventually rises bearing numerous nodding, satin-textured flowers that range from clear red through pink and purple to occasional blue or white forms depending on the seed strain. Native to shaded ravines and forest margins across the Himalaya at roughly 2500-4000m, it needs cool, humid summers and consistently moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to perform well. Most plants are monocarpic, building a rosette for one or two seasons before flowering heavily and then dying, so growing from fresh seed obtained through specialist alpine or woodland seed exchanges is the standard way to keep it in the garden, since named clones do not propagate reliably from cuttings or division. Protect young rosettes from winter waterlogging, which is a more common cause of loss than cold itself.

common_name: Low's Pitcher Plant (Bornean Montane Pitcher Plant)

planting.note: Pot tissue-cultured starts into a loose, mineral-poor mix of long-fiber sphagnum moss and perlite or orchid bark, and give it cooler night temperatures and higher humidity than lowland Nepenthes species need.

directions: Nepenthes lowii is unmistakable for its dimorphic pitchers: ground-level pitchers function as ordinary insect traps, while the unusual upper, aerial pitchers are large, flared, and hourglass-shaped, lacking a normal insect-catching rim and instead positioned beneath overhanging foliage where mountain tree shrews feed on sugary secretions and leave droppings that the plant absorbs as a nitrogen source. It grows naturally on Mount Kinabalu, Mount Tambuyukon, and Mount Trusmadi in Sabah, Borneo, at roughly 1650-2600m in cool, perpetually humid montane forest. Cultivated plants are produced by specialist carnivorous plant nurseries through tissue culture rather than wild collection, and need bright but indirect light, consistently high humidity, and an open, mineral-poor substrate such as long-fiber sphagnum moss kept evenly moist. A clear day-to-night temperature drop, mimicking its mountain habitat, encourages the best pitcher production.
